newsitem.title: UK: Cost of misselling compensation set to rise again.
newsitem.headline: Cost of misselling compensation set to rise again.

text.p: British insurance companies face a sharp rise in the cost of compensating victims of pension misselling after financial watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) confirmed it would be taking account of the abolition of advanced corporation tax (ACT) at last week's budget.

The costs of compensation could eventually rise by as much as 500 million pounds ($843.5 million) sending the final bill for the industry well above the four billion pounds previously estimated, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI).
Companies who wrongly advised customers to leave occupational pension schemes in the late 1980s and early 1990s have offered to match the benefits of the schemes left.
The changes to ACT will mean having to contribute more into occupational schemes to buy people back in.
Administrative costs associated with coping with the changes are also likely to rise, pushing bills even higher.
An ABI spokeswoman warned that the whole review process could be slowed further because some cases will have to be looked at anew in the light of the ACT changes.
Even cases where someone had gone back into an occupational scheme and insurers had arranged an amount to contribute may now need to be looked at again.
More than one and a half a million people may have been wrongly advised to take out personal pensions instead of staying with occupational schemes between 1988 and 1994.

Companies have come under increasing pressure from the government and regulators in recent months to speed up compensation payments to those who lost out including a policy of "naming and shaming" firms suspected of dragging their feet.
In 1994 the SIB initiated a widespread review of all personal pensions sold since April 1988.
Since then, firms involved have been set a target deadline of the end of 1998 to compensate victims losing out.

The SIB said the revised basis for calculating loss and redress taking into account changes in ACT would be contained in the next quarterly review of rates of return to be published as scheduled on August 1.
The review will also take account of changes in investment conditions during the current quarter, including interest rates, inflation rates and returns on equities and gilts.
The adjustment in respect of ACT will be backdated to July 2, the date of the budget when the change was announced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
Calculations of loss and offers made by firms on or after that date will need to be amended to take the abolition of ACT recovery into account, SIB said. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
